query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings, the wear resistance and microscopic deformation under high‐temperature sliding are governed by the in situ formation of a continuous, protective Cr‐rich oxide layer at the sliding interface. A pre‐oxidation treatment that deliberately promotes the formation of this layer will reduce wear and limit plastic deformation compared to a baseline as-deposited coating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation (annealing) treatment in a mild oxygen environment to promote a continuous Cr-rich surface oxide scale before high-temperature sliding.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., operating temperatures above approximately 600 °C) under conditions where oxidation kinetics are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the controlled pre-oxidation treatment accelerates the formation of a protective oxide scale that reduces direct metal-metal contact during sliding. This scale acts as a barrier to shear and stress concentration, leading to reduced adhesive wear and a mitigation of microscopic plastic deformation. In the absence of this optimized oxide layer (baseline as-deposited condition), localized mechanical damage and subsurface plastic deformation occur more readily.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced subsurface plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without the pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected only under high-temperature sliding conditions where oxidation kinetics allow for the formation of a continuous oxide layer (e.g., above ~600 °C). At lower temperatures, the effect may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of Cr in forming a protective oxide is well established in similar systems, the quantitative degree to which the oxide layer reduces wear in this specific high-entropy alloy and the potential influence of other alloying elements (Fe, Ni, Co, Cu) remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu-coated samples: one set with a controlled pre-oxidation/annealing treatment to induce a continuous Cr-rich oxide layer, and a baseline set without treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., at >600 °C) and quantitatively measure wear rates and subsurface deformation.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to confirm continuous oxide scale formation.
Wear rate quantification via mass loss or profilometry.
Measurement of subsurface plastic deformation (e.g., microhardness profiling, residual stress measurements).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a continuous Cr-rich oxide scale, or if there is no statistically significant reduction in wear rate or extent of plastic deformation compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
